la:verb:allicio.html:
al-lĭcĭo (adl-), lexi, lectum, 3 (acc. to , and P., also adliceo, ēre,
perf. allicui, Piso ap. P., and ), v. a.
lacio
.
Lit., to draw to one's self, to attract (in Cic. freq., elsewhere rare; never in Ter., Hor., or Juv.): Si magnetem lapidem dicam, qui ferrum ad se adliciat et attrahat,.—
Trop.: rex sum, si ego illum hodie hominem ad me adlexero, * : adlicit aurīs, * (Lachm. here reads adficit): adlicere ad misericordiam,: nostris officiis benevolentiam,; so ; : adlicere hominum mentes dicendo,: quae adliciant animum, * ; ; ; ; ; ; : adliciunt somnos tempus motusque merumque,: comibus est oculis adliciendus amor,: gelidas nocturno frigore pestes,: Gallias,; .

la:noun:Allobrox.html:
Allō^brox, ăgis, and plur.Allō^brŏ-ges, um, m. (
acc. sing. Allobroga, ), the Allobroges, in Ptol. Ἀλλόβρυγες, a warlike people in Gallia Narbonensis, on the east side of the Rhone, and to the north of l'Isère, now Savoy, Dép. de l'Isère, and a part of the Dép. de l'Ain, ; ; ; ; cf. Mann. Gall. 57 and 91.—The sing. is found only in the poets, : qui totiens Ciceronem Allobroga (i. e. barbare loquentem) dixit,.—Hence, deriv. adj.: Allō^brŏgĭcus, a, um, Allobrogian: vinum,: vitis,—Hence, a surname of Q. Fabius Maximus, as conqueror of the Allobroges, .

la:verb:alligo.gloss: to bind to, up or around something, tie, fetter, fasten; bandage
senses: to bind to, up or around something, tie, fetter, fasten; bandage
la:verb:alligo.html:
al-lĭgo (adl-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
Lit., to bind to something: ad statuam,: ad palum,, § 71; so in the witticism of Cic.: Quis generum meum ad gladium adligavit?: leones adligati,. —In Col. of binding the vine to trees or other supports, 4, 13; so .—
In gen., to bind, to bind up, bind round: dolia,. So of the binding up of wounds: vulnus, Poët. ap. : adligatum vulnus,: oculus adligatus,.—Of the binding of the hands, feet, etc.: adliga, inquam, colliga,: cum adligāsset Isaac filium,; : adligari se ac venire patitur,: adligetur vinculo ferreo,: catenis,.—Hence, allĭgāti (adl-) (sc. servi), slaves that are fettered, .—Of other things: adligare caput lanā,: adligat (naves) ancora, makes or holds fast, .—In Plin. of fixing colors, to fix, make fast: (alga) ita colorem adligans, ut elui postea non possit, 32, 6, 22, § 66; 9, 38, 62, § 134.—Poet.: lac adligatum,curdled,.—
Trop., to bind, to hold fast, to hinder, detain; or in a moral sense, to bind, to oblige, lay under obligation (cf. obligo; very freq., but in the class. per. for the most part only in more elevated prose): caput suum,: jure jurando adligare aliquem,; : hic furti se adligat,shows himself guilty, (astringit, illaqueat, et obnoxium facit, Don.; cf. : homo furti se astringet,; for this gen. cf. Roby, § 1324): adligare se scelere,: adligatus sponsu,: nuptiis adligari,: lex omnes mortales adligat,: non modo beneficio sed etiam benevolentiae significatione adligari,: stipulatione adligari,: more majorum,: ne existiment ita se adligatos, ut, etc.,: ne forte quā re impediar et adliger,— With dat. (eccl. Lat.): adligatus es uxori,: legi,; (= lege).—* Adligatus calculus, in games of chess,a piece that cannot be moved,

la:verb:allecto.html:
allecto (adl-), āvi, ātum, 1,
v. freq. [id.], to allure, to entice (prob. only in the foll. exs.): ad agrum fruendum non modo non retardat, verum etiam invitat atque adlectat senectus,; : boves sibilo,.

la:other:Allia.gloss: a river in Latium, famous for its battle
senses: a river in Latium, famous for its battle
la:other:Allia.html:
Allĭa (more correct than Alĭa; cf. Wagner, Orthogr. Vergil. p. 415 sq.), ae, f.,
a little river eleven miles northwards from Rome, near Crustumerium, in the country of the Sabines, passing through a wide plain (cf. Mann. Ital. 1, 520; Müll. Roms Camp. 1, 138; 141 sq.); it was made memorable by the terrible defeat of the Romans by the Gauls A. U. C. 365, XV. Kal. Sextil. (18 July).—Hence, Alliensis, e, adj., of or pertaining to Allia: dies, of this battle, considered ever after as a dies nefastus, -39; 6, 1; ; ; ; ; cf. Paul. ex Müll.

la:noun:allegoria.html:
allēgŏrĭa, ae, f., = ἀλληγορία,
an allegory, i. e. a figurative representation of a thought or of an abstract truth, under an image carried through to the end: continuus (usus comparationis) in allegoriam et aenigmata exit,; so : quae sunt per allegoriam dicta,are spoken allegorically,: allegoriarum explanationes, (in Cic. written in Greek, Or. 27, 94; ).

la:verb:alloquor.gloss: to speak to, address; salute, greet
senses: to speak to, address; salute, greet
to appeal to the gods in thanksgiving and prayer
la:verb:alloquor.html:
al-lŏquor (adl-), cūtus, 3,
v. dep. a.: aliquem, to speak to, to address, esp. used in greeting, admonishing, consoling. etc.; hence also, to salute; to exhort, rouse; to console (cf. in Gr. παραμυθέομαι; in the ante-class. and class. per. rare; in Cic. only twice; more freq. from the time of the Aug. poets).
To speak to, to address: quem ore funesto adloquar? Att. ap. : admones et adloqueris,: hominem blande adloqui,; so : quem nemo adloqui vellet,; so Auct. ad ; ; ; ; 13, 739; : senatum, compositā in magnificentiam oratione, adlocutus,; so ; : adlocutus est (eis) linguā Hebraeā,; .—
Esp.
To address the gods in thanksgiving and prayer: dis gratias agere atque adloqui,; ; so, patriam adlocuta maestast ita voce miseriter,.—
To address, as a general his troops, to exhort, to rouse: quae ubi consul accepit, sibimetipsi circumeundos adloquendosque milites ratus, Liv, 10, 35: (Alexander) variā oratione milites adloquebatur,: neque milites adlocuturo etc.,; . —
In consolation, to speak to, to console, to comfort: adlocutum mulieres ire aiunt, cum eunt ad aliquam locutum consolandi causā,: adloqui in luctu,: adflictum adloqui caput, P. and R.

la:verb:allego.gloss: to send someone away with a commission or charge, despatch, depute, employ, commission
senses: to send someone away with a commission or charge, despatch, depute, employ, commission
to instigate someone to an act of fraud or deceit
to bring forward, relate, recount, mention, adduce; urge, plead
la:verb:allego.html:
al-lēgo (adl-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
To send one away with a commission or charge, to despatch, depute, commission (of private business, while legare is used in a similar signif. of State affairs; most freq. in Plaut.; elsewhere rare, but class.): ne illi aliquem adlegent, qui mi os occillet, (cf. delegare, prol. 67 and 83); so ; ; ; ; : ego si adlegāssem aliquem ad hoc negotium,: alium ego isti rei adlegabo,: amicos adlegat,: homines nobiles adlegat iis, qui peterent, ne, etc.,: adlegarem te ad illos, qui, etc.,; so fin.: cum patrem primo adlegando, deinde coram ipse rogando fatigāsset, first by the friends sent, and then by personal entreaties, etc., Gron. —Hence, allēgāti (adl-), ōrum, m., deputies: inter adlegatos Oppianici,; .—
Sometimes in the sense of subornare, to instigate or incite one to an act of fraud or deceit: eum adlegaverunt, suum qui servum diceret cum auro esse apud me,: ut ne credas a me adlegatum hunc senem, * Ruhnk.; cf. allegatus.—
To bring forward, to relate, recount, mention, adduce (post-Aug.): exemplum,: hoc senatui adlegandum putasti,: decreta,fin.: merita,; so : priorem se petitum ab Alexandro adlegat,; .—And in a zeugma: (legati) munera, preces, mandata regis sui adlegant, they bring or offer the gifts, entreaties, and mandates, ; cf.: orationem et per incensum deprecationem adlegans,: adlegare se ex servitute in ingenuitatem, a legal phrase, to release one's self from servitude by adducing reasons, proofs, etc., .

senses: an accession of land gradually washed to the shore by the flowing of water
la:noun:alluvio.html:
allŭvĭo (adl-), ōnis, f.
id.
.
In gen., a washing upon, an overflowing, an inundation: adluvione paulatim terra consumitur,: terra aquarum saepe adluvionibus mersa,.—
In the jurists, an accession of land gradually washed to the shore by the flowing of water, alluvial land: quod per adluvionem agro nostro flumen adjecit, jure gentium nobis adquiritur,; —Hence, jura adluvionum et circumluvio num, ; cf. .

allēgŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀλληγορικός,
allegorical: lex,: ambages,.—Adv.: allēgŏrĭcē, allegorically, ; ; Aug. ad Genes. tit. 4, 28.

allĭgātĭo (adl-), ōnis, f.
id.

Abstr. pro concr., a band, ; so .

la:verb:allido.html:
al-līdo (adl-), si, sum, 3, v. a.
laedo
,
to strike or dash one thing upon or against another.
Lit.: tetra ad saxa adlidere, Att. ap. : ut si quis, prius arida quam sit Cretea persona, adlidat pilaeve trabive, who dashes an image of clay against a post, etc., ; so : (remigum) pars ad scopulos adlisa,; so : in latus adlisis clupeis,.—Absol., ; cf. Schneid. ad h. 1; ; .—
Trop., to bring into danger; pass., to suffer damage (the figure taken from a shipwreck; cf. affligo): in quibus (damnationibus) Servius adlisus est,; so : dixerunt, si fundus praevaleat, adlidi dominum,.

la:verb:allevo.gloss: to lift or set up, raise
senses: to lift or set up, raise
to lighten, lessen, alleviate, mitigate, reduce
to raise up, make distinguished; enhance
la:verb:allevo.html:
al-lĕvo (adl-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
1. lĕvo
.
Lit., to lift up, to raise on high, to raise, set up (in the ante-Aug. per. very rare, perh. only twice in Sall. and Hirt.; later often, esp. in Quint. and the histt.): quibus (laqueis) adlevati milites facilius ascenderent, * : pauci elevati scutis, borne up on their shields (others: adlevatis scutis, with uplifted shields, viz. for protection against the darts of the enemy), Auct. B. Alex. 20: gelidos complexibus adlevat artus,: cubito adlevat artus,: naves turribus atque tabulatis adlevatae,: supercilia adlevare, (cf. the Gr. τὰς ὀφρῦς ἀνασπᾶν); so, bracchium,: pollicem,: manum,; : oculos,: faciem alicujus manu,: adlevavit eum, lifted him up (of the lame man), —
Trop.
To lighten, alleviate, mitigate physical or mental troubles; or, referring to the individual who suffers, to lift up, sustain, comfort, console (class.): aliorum aerumnam dictis adlevans, old poet in (cf. Sophocl. Fragm. ap. Brunck. p. 588: Καλῶς κακῶς πράσσοντι συμπαραινέσας): ubi se adlevat, ibi me adlevat, * : Allevat Dominus omnes, qui corruunt,: dejecistis eos, dum adlevarentur,: onus, aliquā ex parte,: sollicitudines,: adlevor cum loquor tecum absens,: adlevare corpus, id. ; : adlevor animum (poet.), .—
To diminish the force or weight of a thing, to lessen, lighten: adversariorum confirmatio diluitur aut infirmatur aut adlevatur,: adlevatae notae,removed,.—
To raise up, i. e. to make distinguished; pass., to be or become distinguished: C. Caesar eloquentiā et spiritu et jam consulatu adlevabatur,.

la:verb:alludo.html:
al-lūdo (adl-), ūsi, ūsum, 3, v. a. and n.
To play or sport with any thing, to joke, jest, to do a thing sportively; with ad or dat. (most freq. after the Aug. per.; never in Plaut.; and in Ter. and in Cic. only once), * : Galba autem adludens (discoursing in jests) varie et copiose multas similitudines adferre, : occupato,; : nec plura adludens,: Cicero Trebatio adludens,jesting with, Spald., Halm; so —
Trop., of the motion,
Of the waves, to sport with, to play against, dash upon: mare terram appetens litoribus adludit,: solebat Aquilius, quid esset litus, ita definire, quā fluctus adluderet (B. and K. read eluderet; v. eludo), ; cf. : in adludentibus undis,.—With acc.: omnia, quae ... fluctus salis adludebant,.—
Of the wind, to play with: summa cacumina silvae lenibus adludit flabris levis Auster,: tremens Adludit patulis arbor hiatibus,.
la:verb:alludo.inflection: ūsi, ūsum, 3, v. a. and n.

la:verb:allubesco.html:
al-lŭbesco (adl-), ĕre,
v. inch. [lubet].
With dat., to be pleasing to (post-class.): illa basiare volenti promptis saviolis adlubescebat,; .—*
Absol.: Hercle vero jam adlubescit (femina) primulum,: adlubescere aquis,to find pleasure in, to drink with pleasure,.

la:noun:allus.html: allus, i, m.: pollex scandens proximum digitum, quod velut insiluisse in alium videtur, quod Graece ἅλλεσθαι dicitur, Paul. ex Müll.; kindr. with allex, q. v.

la:verb:allevio.html:
al-lĕvio (adl-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
lĕvis
, = allĕvo,
to make light, to lighten.
Lit.: ut (navis) alleviaretur ab eis,; .—
Trop., to raise up, relieve: alleviabit eum Dominus,: curas alicui,.—Spec.: alleviata est terra Zabulon,is dealt lightly, leniently with,.

senses: to bathe (of the sea or waves)
la:verb:alluo.html:
al-lŭo (adl-), ŭi, 3, v. n.,
to flow near to, to wash against, to bathe, of the sea, the waves, etc. (perh. not used before the Cic. per.).
Lit.: non adluuntur a mari moenia,: ita jactantur fluctibus, ut numquam adluantur,: fluvius latera haec adluit,: flumen quo adluitur oppidum,; : amnis ora vicina adluens,: adluit gentes Maeotis,.—
Fig.: (Massilia) cincta Gallorum gentibus barbariae fluctibus adluitur,.
